title: Sit in the dust of the wise (Avot 1:4)
word: Sit in the dust of the wise
hook: let your house be a meeting place for the wise; drink their words with thirst

segments.voice: Yesterday, Antigonus: serve not for the reward. Your line was not for the prize. Did you do one good thing and tell no one? Today, the chain passes to two men named Yose, and the first one talks about dust. Day two hundred thirty-seven.

Picture the difference. One person watches a cooking video at double speed while answering email. Another stands in a grandmother's kitchen for an afternoon, flour on her shirt, watching how the dough is folded, asking why, getting told to be quiet and watch. Both are learning. Only one of them is getting dirty. Real learning has always been a little messy. It means getting close, being the least important person in the room, and wanting it badly. An old sage put all of that into one dusty picture. Today: sit in the dust.
screen: `VIDEO AT DOUBLE SPEED.` → `FLOUR ON YOUR SHIRT.` → `LEARNING GETS DIRTY.`

segments.voice: After Antigonus, Avot's chain passes to pairs of teachers. The first pair: Yose ben Yoezer and Yose ben Yochanan. Yose ben Yoezer says three things, in paraphrase. Let your house be a meeting place for the wise. Sit in the dust of their feet. And drink in their words with thirst. Start with the house. Not the synagogue, not the school. Your house. Make your kitchen table a place where wise people want to come and talk. Then the dust. The commentators give two pictures. In the old academies, students sat on the ground while the teacher sat above them, so you'd literally be in the dust at their feet. Or, the students walked behind their teacher on dirt roads, close enough to catch every word, and got covered in the dust his feet kicked up. Either way: humble, close, and a bit dirty. And here's a detail a scholar loves. The Hebrew verb, mitabek, comes from avak, dust. It's related to the word used when Jacob wrestled the angel all night, the two of them rolling in the dust. So sitting in the dust of the wise isn't just sitting still. It can mean wrestling with them. Asking hard questions. Pushing back. Last, drink their words with thirst. Not polite sipping. The way you drink after a long run, gulping, grateful. Wisdom goes in best when you really want it. A house that welcomes, a student who gets close, and real thirst.
screen: `YOUR HOUSE, A MEETING PLACE.` · `AT THEIR FEET, OR ON THEIR ROAD.` · `MITABEK — TO WRESTLE IN DUST.` · `DRINK WITH THIRST.` · then, large: `SIT IN THE DUST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn from someone older. Settle, and breathe. Think of an older person in your life who knows something you don't. A grandparent, a neighbor, a senior colleague, the old man at the hardware store. What could they teach you? A recipe, a trade, a story, how they got through a hard year. Picture sitting near them, asking, and really listening, thirsty. Decide when you'll ask. The bell holds the time.
Sit in the dust of the wise. Yose ben Yoezer's saying in Avot: open your house to the wise, get close to them, and drink in their words with thirst.
screen: `SIT IN THE DUST OF THE WISE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: sit in the dust. Today, ask someone older one real question, then stop talking and listen all the way to the end. Day two hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Many Jews host study sessions and invite teachers into their homes, and traditional learning is often done in pairs or small circles close to a teacher, arguing as well as listening.

original.note: Hebrew: sit, or wrestle, in the dust of their feet (Avot 1:4).

trapdoor: what you thought: be humble in front of teachers.
what it means: get close to the wise, host them at home, and learn hungrily, even messily.
what a scholar hears: mitabek comes from avak, dust, a root tied to Jacob's all-night wrestling (Genesis 32:25), so the phrase can mean wrestling with teachers too.

notes: Two pictures of 'dust' (sitting on the ground before the teacher; following behind on the road) from memory of Bartenura and others; confirm.
Link of mitabek/avak to vaye'avek (Genesis 32:25) is a common homiletic reading; confirm framing.
Yose ben Yoezer of Tzeredah and Yose ben Yochanan of Jerusalem as the first of the zugot (pairs).
